question.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ f(t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=4+\text{i}.$*
question.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=4+\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=4+\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 1 \\ -1 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(4+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(4+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}({e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ {e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
